messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John had always taken pride in his work as a bank teller. He was meticulous and careful, never wanting to make mistakes that could affect others. But one day, in a moment of distraction, he accidentally triggered the security system, causing a severe injury to a colleague who was caught off guard. The incident left John shaken, and over time, it began to unravel his sense of self. As he navigated his daily routine, John found himself on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. He had difficulty falling asleep at night, lying awake as his mind replayed the incident, rehashing what he could have done differently. Even in safe spaces, like his own home, John felt a persistent sense of unease, unable to shake the feeling that something was off. These feelings of hypervigilance and sleep vigilance made him feel like he was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the next trigger would set him off. When someone touched him unexpectedly, even his wife, John's nerves would fray. He couldn't explain why it affected him so deeply, but being caught off guard brought back the same terror he felt in those chaotic moments after the incident. His reactions since then only served to reinforce his growing sense of inadequacy – he was no longer the reliable, competent person he once thought himself to be. As John's self-doubt grew, memories of that fateful day began to surface more frequently, accompanied by crushing guilt and a deep-seated fear that he had permanently changed for the worse. These memories would often return unbidden, sudden pieces of the incident flashing before his eyes like snapshots. When they did, John felt himself transported back to the scene, reliving the horror and panic. His mind told him he was in danger, that something terrible was about to happen again, and this conviction only intensified his hypervigilance. As these fragments resurfaced, John's perception of himself as a "lousy coper" solidified – why else would these memories still have such power over him? This self-perception, in turn, heightened his sensitivity to triggers: related people, stress, and unexpected touch all took on a menacing quality. At work, John found it increasingly difficult to interact with customers or even his own family. His wife noticed the change in him, but he couldn't explain why he was so distant, so preoccupied. Even simple tasks like counting money or answering questions made him anxious, as if he were waiting for the other shoe to drop. As these difficulties accumulated, John began to see himself as irreparably damaged – a permanent victim of his own carelessness. This sense of hopelessness finally brought him to seek help, though what frightened him most was that therapy would reveal even more evidence of his inadequacy. John's greatest fear now is that he will never be able to shake the memories of that incident or quiet the voice that tells him he's a failure. He hopes that with therapy, he can learn to calm the hypervigilance and rebuild some semblance of control over his life – but for now, those goals feel as elusive as ever.
